textbookText: 1. Family : Brassicaceae (Cruciferae) – Mustard family

Habit and Habitat : The members of this family are annual, biennial or perennial herbs with sulphur smelling. The plants may be cosmopolitan in distribution. Majority of them are common in north temperate region. Vegetative characters:
a. Root: tap, branched, may be modified into fusiform (Raphanus sativus – radish) or napiform (Brassica rapa – turnip)
b. Stem: usually the stem is herbaceous; erect or prostrate, branched, solid, cylindrical, pubescent (hairy)

c. Leaves: Radical (arise from base of stem or underground stem) or cauline (attached directly to main stem nodes) or ramal (found on branches), simple, alternate, exstipulate, petiolate or sessile, lyrate, reticulate venation
Floral Characters
a. Inflorescence: Racemose
b. Flower: Mostly ebracteate, pedicellate, bisexual, complete, actinomorphic rarely
zygomorphic, hypogynous
c. Calyx: 4 sepals, polysepalous, arranged in two whorls, petaloid or sepaloid, imbricate
aestivation, inferior
d. Corolla: 4 petals, polypetalous and cruciform (arranged cross-like), valvate aestivation
e. Androecium: 6 stamens arranged in two whorls, tetradynamous (outer two stamens are
short while inner four are long), anther bilobed, basifixed, introrse
f. Gynoecium: 2 carpels, syncarpous (carpels are united), unilocular in early stage and
later becomes bilocular due to development of false septum, ovary superior, parietal
placentation,
g. Fruits: siliqua or silicula,
h. Pollination: entomophilous (i.e. through insects)
i. Floral Formula: Ebr
j. Floral Diagram:

Economic Importance: i. Brassica campestris (mustard) cultivated to extract the oils used for cooking, burning etc. ii. The plants like turnip, radhish, cabbage etc. are cultivated for vegetables. iii. Seeds of some plants are used as condiments.

iv. Lepidium sativum (chamsur) is used as vegetable as well as in the treatment of asthma, cough and bleeding piles. v. Some plants of this family are grown as an ornamental plant.

Some important plant of this family: a. Mustard – Brassica campestris b. Cauliflower – Brassica oleracea var. botrytis c. Cabbage – Brassica oleracea var. capitata d. Turnip – Brassica rapa e. Radish – Raphanus sativus

2. Family: Fabaceae (Leguminosae) – Legume family Habit and Habitat : The members of this family may be herbs, shrubs, rarely trees. Usually the plants are cultivated for pulses and green manuring. They are cosmopolitan in distribution usually in temperate regions of both northern and southern hemispheres.

Vegetative characters: a. Root: tap root, branched, root bears nodules having nitrogen fixing bacteria. b. Stem: Herbaceous or woody, erect or climbing, branched, angular or cylindrical c. Leaves: Cauline or ramal, compound rarely simple, alternate rarely opposite or whorled, stipulate, petiolate, reticulate venation.

Floral Characters a. Inflorescence: Racemose b. Flower: bracteate or ebracteate, Pedicellate, zygomorphic, bisexual, complete, hypogynous c. Calyx: 5 sepals, gamosepalous, asending imbricate or valvate aestivation d. Corolla: 5 petals (unequal), the uppermost largest petal (known as vexillum or standard), the two free lateral petals (known as wings or alae) and anterior two united petals (known as keel or carina), descending imbricate or vexillary aestivation e. Androecium: 10 stamens, diadelphous of 1+9, one stamen is free remaining nine in bundle partially fused, anther bilobed, basifixed or dorsifixed, introrse. f. Gynoecium: 1 carpel, unilocular, Ovary superior, marginal placentation g. Fruits: legume or pod h. Pollination: entomophilous i. Floral Formula: Br or Ebr % K(5) C1+2+(2) A1+(9) G1 j. Floral Diagram:

3. Family: Solanaceae – Potato family

Habit and Habitat : The members of this family may be annual or perennial herbs, shrubs rarely trees. They are worldwide in distribution most commonly found in tropical and subtropical region of world.

Vegetative characters: a. Root: tap root, branched b. Stem: herbaceous rarely woody, erect or climbing, branched, cylindrical, solid or rarely fistular (hollow), pubescent or glabrous (smooth without hair), sometimes modified underground stem (like tuber in potato). c. Leaves: Cauline or ramal, exstipulate, simple rarely pinnately compound, alternate or opposite in floral region, rarely whorled, petiolate, reticulate venation.
